Marked Magnetic Action Rigidity

Louis-Brahim Beaufort Address: Université Paris-Saclay, Laboratoire de mathématiques d’Orsay, 91405, Orsay, France. Email address: louis-brahim.beaufort@math.cnrs.fr , Sebastián Muñoz-Thon Address: Université Paris-Saclay, Laboratoire de mathématiques d’Orsay, 91405, Orsay, France. Email address: sebastian.munoz-thon@universite-paris-saclay.fr and Sean Richardson Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98195. Email address: seanhr@uw.edu
Abstract.

An exact magnetic system over a closed manifold MM consists of a pair (g,α)(g,\alpha), where gg is a Riemannian metric and α\alpha is a 1-form encoding a magnetic field. In this context, we consider a generalization of the marked length rigidity conjecture: does the marked magnetic action spectrum of magnetic systems with Anosov magnetic flow determine the metric and the 1-form, up to a natural obstruction? In this article we answer this question in two settings: 1) locally for systems with close metrics and 1-forms and 2) for metrics in the same conformal class.

Key words and phrases:
Magnetic geodesics, Magnetic action, Rigidity, X-ray transform
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
37D20, 37D40

1. Introduction

Given a Riemannian manifold MM with Anosov geodesic flow, there exists a unique length-minimizing geodesic in each free homotopy class. The marked length spectrum is the map that assigns to each free homotopy class the length of the minimizing geodesic in it. The Burns–Katok conjecture [5] asks if this map determines the metric gg up to a natural obstruction (a diffeomorphism of MM homotopic to the identity).

In this article, we give partial answers to the magnetic version of this conjecture. An exact magnetic system on MM consists of a pairing (g,α)(g,\alpha) of a Riemannian metric gg with a 1-form α\alpha. We define the Lorentz force as the map Y:T​M→T​MY\colon TM\to TM by

d​αx​(v,w)=gx​(w,Yx​(v)),d\alpha_{x}(v,w)=g_{x}(w,Y_{x}(v)),

where v,w∈Tx​Mv,w\in T_{x}M. A magnetic geodesic is a curve γ:[0,T]→M\gamma\colon[0,T]\to M with acceleration governed by the Lorentz force

(1.1) ∇γ˙γ˙​(t)=Yγ⁡(t)​(γ˙​(t))\nabla_{\dot{\gamma}}\dot{\gamma}(t)=Y_{\gamma(t)}(\dot{\gamma}(t))

where ∇\nabla is the covariant derivative induced by the Levi-Civita connection of gg. Equation (1.1) defines a flow φt:S​M→S​M\varphi_{t}\colon SM\to SM over the unit tangent bundle S​M={(x,v)∈T​M:|v|g=1}SM=\{(x,v)\in TM:|v|_{g}=1\} called the magnetic flow. We will work with magnetic flows that are Anosov (see Section 2). Given a smooth curve γ:[0,T]→M\gamma\colon[0,T]\to M, the (time-free) action with respect to the magnetic system (g,α)(g,\alpha) is given by

𝔸⁡(γ)=𝔸g,α​(γ)=12​∫|γ˙|g2+T2−∫γα.\mathbb{A}(\gamma)=\mathbb{A}_{g,\alpha}(\gamma)=\frac{1}{2}\int|\dot{\gamma}|_{g}^{2}+\frac{T}{2}-\int_{\gamma}\alpha.

This is a natural action to consider as it is the action used in Mañé’s action potential at critical energy level 1/21/2, see [28, 9, 6]. Importantly, in every non-trivial free homotopy class cc, there is a unique minimizer of 𝔸\mathbb{A}, which will be a unit-speed magnetic geodesic γg,α​(c)\gamma_{g,\alpha}(c) [9]*Theorem 29. It is a quick exercise to verify that in the case of an everywhere vanishing magnetic field, these minimizing values are precisely the lengths of the closed geodesics. Thus, in similar fashion to how [12] considers a generalization of the boundary rigidity problem using this action, we consider the following natural generalization of the marked length spectrum to the magnetic setting. Letting 𝒞\mathcal{C} denote the set of free homotopy classes on MM, we define the marked magnetic action as the map

𝒞→ℝ,c↦𝔸g,α​(γg,α​(c)).\displaystyle\mathcal{C}\to\mathbb{R},\quad\quad c\mapsto\mathbb{A}_{g,\alpha}(\gamma_{g,\alpha}(c)).

It is not hard to see that 𝔸\mathbb{A} is invariant under the action by pullback of a diffeomorphism homotopic to the identity, and the addition of an exact 1-form to α\alpha, thus 𝔸g,α​(c)=𝔸ϕ∗​g,ϕ∗​α+d​φ​(c)\mathbb{A}_{g,\alpha}(c)=\mathbb{A}_{\phi^{*}g,\phi^{*}\alpha+d\varphi}(c). Hence, as a natural generalization of the marked length spectrum rigidity conjecture, we consider the following:

Question 1.

Does (𝔸⁡(γ⁡(c)))c∈𝒞(\mathbb{A}(\gamma(c)))_{c\in\mathcal{C}} determine (g,α)(g,\alpha) up to a diffeomorphism homotopic to the identity and an exact closed form?

In this article, we answer Question 1 in two cases. First, we consider magnetic systems in a small neighborhood of a fixed system with solenoidal-injective magnetic X-ray transform I2I_{2} (see Section 2.2). Using a stability estimate obtained in [30], we are able to provide the following local result analogous to the main result of [22] for the geodesic case.

Theorem 1.1.

Let (M,g0,α0)(M,g_{0},\alpha_{0}) be a CkC^{k}-Anosov magnetic system, whose magnetic X-ray transform I2I_{2} is solenoidal-injective. There exist N,ε>0N,\varepsilon>0 such that the following holds. Let (g,α)(g,\alpha) be a magnetic system with the same marked magnetic action as (g0,α0)(g_{0},\alpha_{0}), and such that

‖g−g0‖CN​(M)+‖α−α0‖CN​(M)≤ε.\|g-g_{0}\|_{C^{N}(M)}+\|\alpha-\alpha_{0}\|_{C^{N}(M)}\leq\varepsilon.

Then there exists a diffeomorphism ϕ:M→M\phi\colon M\to M isotopic to the identity, and an exact form d​φd\varphi such that

(g,α)=(ϕ∗​g0,ϕ∗​α0+d​φ).(g,\alpha)=(\phi^{*}g_{0},\phi^{*}\alpha_{0}+d\varphi).

A key difficulty in generalizing from the geodesic flow to the magnetic case is that the linearization argument requires a coupling [g,α][g,\alpha] of a symmetric 2-tensor with a 1-tensor. Such a coupling is also required for the magnetic versions of the potential, divergence, and normal operators, so we have a coupling of Fourier modes throughout our argument.

We now discuss sufficient conditions for solenoidal-injectivity of the magnetic X-ray transform acting on symmetric tensors of order ≤2\leq 2. It was shown in [1] that it is injective on surfaces. In higher dimensions, two similar criteria exist in the literature. The first one is obtained in [12] on manifolds with boundary, and was translated recently to closed manifolds in [30]. Denote, for (x,v)∈S​M(x,v)\in SM,

kx​(v)=supz∈Sx​M,z⟂v2​ℛ​(z,v,v,z)+g​(Yx​(v),z)2+(n+3)​|Yx​z|g2−2​g​((∇xYp)​(v),z),\displaystyle k_{x}(v)=\sup_{z\in S_{x}M,z\perp v}2\mathcal{R}(z,v,v,z)+g(Y_{x}(v),z)^{2}+(n+3)|Y_{x}z|_{g}^{2}-2g((\nabla_{x}Y_{p})(v),z),

where ℛ\mathcal{R} the Riemann curvature tensor. Then, if for any closed orbit γ\gamma with period TγT_{\gamma}, we have

(1.2) Tγ​∫0Tγmax⁡(0,k⁡(γ⁡(t),γ˙​(t))​𝑑t≤4CLOSE,\displaystyle T_{\gamma}\int_{0}^{T_{\gamma}}\max(0,k(\gamma(t),\dot{\gamma}(t))dt\leq 4,

The second criterion was obtained in [4] and may be expressed in terms of the magnetic sectional curvature secg,α\mathrm{sec}^{g,\alpha} recently introduced in [3], which is defined as follows. For v,z∈Sx​Mv,z\in S_{x}M, x∈Mx\in M,

Let (M,g0,α0)(M,g_{0},\alpha_{0}) be an Anosov magnetic system. Assume either

  1. (1)

    MM is a surface.

  2. (2)

    dimM≥3\dim M\geq 3 and either (1.2) or (1.4) holds.

There exists N,ε>0N,\varepsilon>0 such that the following holds. Let (g,α)(g,\alpha) be a magnetic system with the same marked magnetic action as (g0,α)(g_{0},\alpha), and such that

Our second rigidity result deals with magnetic systems in a given conformal class. In this case, we obtain a full answer.

Theorem 1.5.

Let (g1,α1)(g_{1},\alpha_{1}) (g2,α2)(g_{2},\alpha_{2}) be Anosov magnetic systems with the same marked action spectrum. If g1g_{1} is conformal to g2g_{2}, i.e., if there exists f∈C∞​(M)f\in C^{\infty}(M) so that g2=e2​f​g1g_{2}=e^{2f}g_{1}, then f≡0f\equiv 0 and α2=α1+d​φ\alpha_{2}=\alpha_{1}+d\varphi, for some φ∈C∞​(M)\varphi\in C^{\infty}(M).

1.1. Perspectives and related results

The Burns–Katok conjecture [5] has been solved in several cases, although is wide open in higher dimensions. To begin with, Katok [25] solved the conjecture on a fixed conformal class. In the case of negatively curved surfaces, a solution was given by Croke [11] and Otal [31]. A deformation result was given by Croke and Sharafutdinov as a consequence of the injectivity of the X-ray transform for manifolds of negative curvature [10]. In the case of locally symmetric spaces, the conjecture was solved by Hamenstädt [24]. After twenty years, there was a breakthrough by Guillarmou and Lefeuvre [22], showing the results for metric that are close enough. The result on surface was recently generalized to the case of Anosov metrics in [21], and has also been studied recently for both magnetic and other dissipative flows [18]. We point out that the result of [18] could hypothetically be generalized along the lines of [21] to obtain a rigidity result on the length of magnetic orbit, but not the magnetic action which we consider here.

In the case of magnetic system on closed manifolds, a deformation result was obtained on surfaces by Marshall Reber [29]. This was recently generalized in [2], where rigidity was proved using the length of magnetic geodesics in place of the action, we discuss this below. The study of the linearized problem i.e., of the magnetic ray transform, that is, the operator that integrates functions (or pair of tensors) over magnetic geodesic (see Section 2.2 for the precise definition) has been studied for 0- and 1-tensors in [13] and [14] on surfaces, and in [15] in the higher dimension case. For 2-tensors, in the case of surfaces, it was studied in [1]. The last two authors studied the case of 2-tensors in [30] under a bound in the sectional curvature and the Lorentz force (which holds, for example, for negatively curved manifolds with small magnetic 1-form in the C2C^{2}-norm). In the forthcoming paper [4], the first author solves the problem for general mm-tensors, under a bound in the magnetic sectional curvature (defined in (1.3)).

Regarding our results, Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 are motivated by the local rigidity result in [22]. In the same way as there, we show that when a magnetic system is close to a given one, we can deform it to a one that is divergence free (or solenoidal, see Section 2.2). We then show that the potential part of the difference vanishes. This last step uses, in a implicit way, microlocal techniques. Indeed, we use stability results for the linearized problem obtained recently by the last two authors [30]. Although our bounds follow the spirit from [22], we avoid using the unstable Jacobian, and we neither use the geodesic stretch as in the proof proposed later in [20] (see also [26]*Chapter 17). Hence, our result also gives a new proof of the local rigidity result by Guillarmou–Lefeuvre by using the stability of the geodesic X-ray transform on closed manifolds. The hypothesis of Theorem 1.2 regarding the dimension of MM or the magnetic sectional curvature, are due to the fact that the stability result from [30] only holds if the linearized problem is solved (i.e., when the magnetic ray transform is solenoidal injective, see Section 2.2 for the proper definitions). Our stability result, Theorem 1.3 is inspired in the analog result for the marked length spectrum from [22], but it can also be related to the approximate and quantitative marked length spectrum results by Butt [7], [8]. As in [22], the proof Theorem 1.3 follows a deformation argument together with the smoothness of the action (presented in Section 3), the stability of the magnetic X-ray transform (Lemma 2.2), and Sobolev estimates.

Our rigidity result in a same conformal class is inspired by the corresponding result in the Riemannian case by Katok [25], and the corresponding result in the case of magnetic systems on manifolds with boundary [12]*Theorem 6.1. The proof of this last result uses Santaló’s formula which is not suitable for closed manifolds. Instead, we argue as in [25] and use the fact that the magnetic flow preserves the Liouville measure, which implies that this measure can be approximated by Dirac masses over closed trajectories of the flow. This together with a Hölder inequality argument, show that the conformal factor is trivial. The relation of the magnetic 1-forms then follows from algebraic manipulations together with an application of the Non-negative Livšic theorem, and the fact that the magnetic X-ray transform acting on 1-forms is injective [15].

Finally, let us mention why we consider the action instead of the length as in [29], [2]. Although the length of closed orbits is more natural from the dynamical point of view, from the physical and analytic one the action is more appropriate. Indeed, magnetic geodesics are minimizers of the action but not of the length. Furthermore, since we use the microlocal methods from [23] and [22] to prove the local result, one has to study first the linearized problem. In the case of the geodesic flow, the linearization of the length gives the geodesic X-ray transform, although in the case of magnetic systems, linearizing the lengths of magnetic geodesics transforms gives birth to an operator that is not of X-ray type. However, the linearization of the action is indeed the magnetic X-ray transform acting on 2- and 1-tensors, a operator that was studied recently by the last two authors [30], generalizing [23]. Finally, we also mention that the rigidity results in the case of manifolds with boundary (which also study the magnetic X-ray transform) [12] also use the action instead of the length, which also served us for a justification to tackle the action rigidity problem instead of the one with the length.

Organization of this article

In Section 2 we introduce the machinery required for this article. In particular, we recall the definition of anisotropic Sobolev spaces associated to Anosov flows, which serve as the natural ambient where Guillarmou’s Π\Pi operator is defined. There we also introduce the magnetic X-ray transform and its associated normal operator defined in terms of Π\Pi. In Section 3 we prove some technical results that will be used in the proof of our local result. Finally, Theorems 1.1, 1.3, and 1.5 are proved in Sections 4, 5, and 6, respectively.

2. Preliminaries

2.1. Anosov flows and Anisotropic Sobolev Spaces

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} a closed manifold, and let φt\varphi_{t} be an Anosov flow on ℳ\mathcal{M} preserving a smooth measure d​μd\mu. Let FF be the generator of φ\varphi. Then, have a continuous flow-invariant splitting

T​ℳ=ℝ​F⊕Es⊕Eu,T\mathcal{M}=\mathbb{R}F\oplus E_{s}\oplus E_{u},

T∗​ℳ=ℝ​E0⊕Es∗⊕Eu∗,T^{*}\mathcal{M}=\mathbb{R}E_{0}\oplus E_{s}^{*}\oplus E_{u}^{*},

ℋ±s​(ℳ):=As∓1​(L2​(ℳ)).\mathcal{H}_{\pm}^{s}(\mathcal{M}):=A_{s}^{\mp 1}(L^{2}(\mathcal{M})).

2.2. Analysis of magnetic flows

In this subsection we introduce operators defined in terms of the magnetic flow. We first recall the definition of the associated X-ray transform. Let [p,q]∈C0​(M,Sm​T∗​M)×C0​(M,Sm−1​T∗​M)[p,q]\in C^{0}(M,S^{m}T^{*}M)\times C^{0}(M,S^{m-1}T^{*}M). We define the magnetic X-ray transform of [p,q][p,q] by

Im​[p,q]​(c)=∫0ℓg​(γ​(c))(πm∗​p+πm−1∗​q)​(φt​(x,v))​𝑑t,I_{m}[p,q](c)=\int_{0}^{\ell_{g}(\gamma(c))}(\pi_{m}^{*}p+\pi_{m-1}^{*}q)(\varphi_{t}(x,v))dt,

where γ⁡(c)\gamma(c) is the unique magnetic geodesic in cc. When we want to emphasize that the X-ray transform corresponds to the one associated to the magnetic system (g,α)(g,\alpha), we will write Im:=Img,αI_{m}:=I_{m}^{g,\alpha}. As it is shown in [12], I2I_{2} corresponds to the linearization of 𝔸\mathbb{A} in the direction [2​p,−q][2p,-q].

We also recall that tensors on a Riemannian manifold MM can be written as a sum of potential plus a divergence free part. In the same fashion, we have a similar decomposition for pair of tensors [p,q]∈C1​(M,Sm​T∗​M)×C1​(M,Sm−1​T∗​M)[p,q]\in C^{1}(M,S^{m}T^{*}M)\times C^{1}(M,S^{m-1}T^{*}M) when MM is endowed with a magnetic system. We present it for m=1,2m=1,2 which is enough for our purposes (see [30]*Section 4 for the general result). We define the magnetic potential and the magnetic divergence by

Dμ:C1​(T∗​M)×C1​(M)→C0​(M,S2​T∗​M)×C0​(T∗​M),Dμ∗:C1​(M,S2​T∗​M)×C1​(T∗​M)→C0​(T∗​M)×C0​(M),\begin{split}D_{\mu}&\colon C^{1}(T^{*}M)\times C^{1}(M)\to C^{0}(M,S^{2}T^{*}M)\times C^{0}(T^{*}M),\\ D_{\mu}^{*}&\colon C^{1}(M,S^{2}T^{*}M)\times C^{1}(T^{*}M)\to C^{0}(T^{*}M)\times C^{0}(M),\end{split}
Dμ=(D0Yd),Dμ∗=(−tr(∇∙)−Y0−tr(∇∙)),D_{\mu}=\begin{pmatrix}D&0\\ Y&d\end{pmatrix},\qquad D_{\mu}^{*}=\begin{pmatrix}-\tr(\nabla\bullet)&-Y\\ 0&-\tr(\nabla\bullet)\end{pmatrix},

respectively. Here DD is the symmetrized covariant derivative, ∇\nabla is the Levi-Civita connection, dd is the exterior differential, and YY is the Lorentz force acting on 1-tensors which is defined by Y​(ξ)x​(v)=ξ⁡(Yx​(v))Y(\xi)_{x}(v)=\xi(Y_{x}(v)), where ξ∈C0​(T∗​M)\xi\in C^{0}(T^{*}M), v∈Tx​Mv\in T_{x}M.

Then, the potential-solenoidal decomposition says that any pair can be written as a the sum of a pair of tensors in the image of DμD_{\mu} together with an element in the kernel of Dμ∗D_{\mu}^{*}.

Furthermore, the decomposition can be used to characterize the kernel of ImI_{m}. We have that ran⁡Dμ⊂Im\ran D_{\mu}\subset I_{m}, and in the case of equality, we say that ImI_{m} is solenoidal injective, which we always abbreviate as s-injective.

After these preliminaries, we are in good shape to state the stability result for the X-ray transform ([30]*Theorem 1.4). This says that we can control the divergence free part of a pair of tensors by its magnetic X-ray transform.

Lemma 2.2 (Stability).

Assume that ImI_{m} is s-injective. There exists s0∈(0,1)s_{0}\in(0,1) and C,τ>0C,\tau>0 such that for all f∈C1​(M,Sm​T∗​M)×C1​(M,Sm−1​T∗​M)f\in C^{1}(M,S^{m}T^{*}M)\times C^{1}(M,S^{m-1}T^{*}M) and s<s0s<s_{0}:

‖πker⁡Dμ∗​f‖Hs0≤C​‖Im​f‖ℓ∞​(𝒞)τ​‖f‖C11−τ.\|\pi_{\ker D_{\mu}^{*}}f\|_{H^{s_{0}}}\leq C\|I_{m}f\|_{\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{C})}^{\tau}\|f\|_{C^{1}}^{1-\tau}.

As was mentioned in the introduction, s-injectivity (and hence, Lemma 2.2) holds when the Riemannian manifold (M,g)(M,g) has negative sectional curvature and α\alpha is C2C^{2}-small enough by the results in [30]*Section 6.

We will also need the operator that plays the role of the normal operator associated to ImI_{m}. As in the case of geodesic flows, it is defined in terms of Guillarmou’s Π\Pi operator. We define the magnetic normal operator

Nm=(πm∗(Π+1⊗1)πm∗πm∗(Π+1⊗1)πm−1∗πm−1∗(Π+1⊗1)πm∗πm−1∗(Π+1⊗1)πm−1∗),N_{m}=\begin{pmatrix}\pi_{m*}(\Pi+1\otimes 1)\pi_{m}^{*}&\pi_{m*}(\Pi+1\otimes 1)\pi_{m-1}^{*}\\ \pi_{m-1*}(\Pi+1\otimes 1)\pi_{m}^{*}&\pi_{m-1*}(\Pi+1\otimes 1)\pi_{m-1}^{*}\end{pmatrix},

The following is a consequence of the pseudodifferential nature of NmN_{m} ([30]*Theorem 1.3).

Lemma 2.3.

Let (M,g,α)(M,g,\alpha) be an Anosov magnetic system. Then for any s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}, NmN_{m} is a continuous map from the space Hs​(M,Sm​T∗​M)×Hs​(M,Sm−1​T∗​M)H^{s}(M,S^{m}T^{*}M)\times H^{s}(M,S^{m-1}T^{*}M) to Hs+1​(M,Sm​T∗​M)×Hs+1​(M,Sm−1​T∗​M)H^{s+1}(M,S^{m}T^{*}M)\times H^{s+1}(M,S^{m-1}T^{*}M).

Finally, we record the following version of a theorem by Lopes and Thieullen [27] for later use.

Lemma 2.4 (Non-negative Livšic Theorem).

Let α∈(0,1]\alpha\in(0,1], and let FF be the generator of an Anosov magnetic flow associated to the magnetic system (g0,α0)(g_{0},\alpha_{0}). There exist a constant C=C⁡(g0,α0)>0C=C(g_{0},\alpha_{0})>0 and r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1) such that for any u∈Cβ​(S​M)u\in C^{\beta}(SM) with non-negative integral over every γ(g0,α0)​(c)\gamma_{(g_{0},\alpha_{0})}(c), there exist h∈Cβ​r​(S​M)h\in C^{\beta r}(SM) and A∈Cβ​r​(S​M)A\in C^{\beta r}(SM) such that A≥0A\geq 0 and u+F​h=Au+Fh=A. Moreover, ‖A‖Cβ​r≤C​‖u‖Cβ\|A\|_{C^{\beta r}}\leq C\|u\|_{C^{\beta}}.

The next ingredient that we need is a reduction to the case of potential tensors: one can deform magnetic systems in a neighborhood of a given one, so that the deformation is solenoidal. The proof on closed Riemannian case goes back to Ebin [17]. For smooth magnetic systems, a proof in the case of manifolds with boundary can be found in [12]*Lemma 6.6.
